messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 51
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Dentist
- Trauma Type: Stalking
- Pcl5: 63

Linh arrives for her appointment exactly on time, as she always does. She sits in the chair with her back to the wall, her purse clutched tight in her lap. Before the session began, she asked if the door could remain slightly open — a request she makes weekly and apologizes for each time. She is a dentist, fifty-one years old, married for twenty-three years, and the mother of two grown children. She speaks in a measured, careful voice, as though she is still deciding how much to reveal.

Two and a half years ago, a male patient — mid-thirties, soft-spoken, always polite — began requesting Linh specifically for his cleanings. At first she thought nothing of it. Many patients preferred her gentle technique. But soon he started asking personal questions: where she grew up, what her husband did, whether she had children. She gave vague answers, changed the subject. Then the gifts appeared: a small box of chocolates left at the reception desk, a hand-written card thanking her for “the light she brought into his life.” The office manager thought it was sweet. Linh felt something cold settle in her stomach.

She told the patient gently that gifts were not appropriate. He agreed, apologized, and seemed to understand. But the next week, he was waiting in the parking lot after her shift. He waved, smiled, and said he happened to be in the area. She told herself it was a coincidence. A week later, he was there again. And again. She stopped parking in the lot and began using a garage two blocks away. He found her there too. That was when she started to feel truly watched — a heavy, invisible pressure at the back of her neck, even inside her own home.

The patient left notes under her windshield wiper, then under the door of her house. He called the dental office repeatedly, asking for her personal schedule. Linh filed a police report. They spoke to him. He denied everything. Without concrete threats, they said, there was little they could do. She transferred to a different clinic across town. She and her husband moved to a new apartment. She changed her phone number, her route to work, her daily routines. But the feeling never left.

Now Linh is always scanning. In the grocery store, she notices every man who walks past the same aisle twice. In her dental chair, with a patient reclined and her hands in their mouth, she sometimes freezes mid-procedure, her heart pounding as she tries to remember if she locked the exam room door. She has started asking her hygienist to stay in the room when she treats any male patient who is roughly the same height and build as the stalker. She cannot explain why, only that her throat closes and her hands shake.

She sleeps poorly — wakes at 3 a.m. thinking she hears footsteps in the hallway. She checks the locks three times before bed, then checks again. Her husband tries to comfort her, but she finds herself pulling away from his touch, feeling unsafe even in their bed. She is irritable with him, snaps at small things, then feels guilty and withdraws further.

At work, she is still competent, but she avoids certain procedures that require prolonged, uninterrupted focus. She has begun delegating more complex cases to a colleague, telling herself it is because she is tired. She is tired. The hypervigilance consumes energy she once had for her family, her hobbies, her patients. She no longer goes to the park for her morning walks. She stopped attending her daughter’s soccer games because the open field felt too exposed.

She tells me all of this without tears, her face composed, but her fingers twist the strap of her purse. She wants to understand why she still feels the stalker’s presence even though she has not seen him in over a year. She is angry at herself — for not being stronger, for not catching him sooner, for letting a stranger steal her peace of mind. She says, “I used to love my work. Now I count the minutes until I can go home and lock the door.”
